904.title: The tongue that did not burn
904.hook: a legend: after his cremation, Kumarajiva's tongue remained, proof his translations were true
904.howItsDone: Chinese Buddhists retell the story of Kumarajiva's tongue as a sign of his faithfulness, and a pagoda associated with the relic is visited in western China.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kumarajiva, the monk from Kucha whose Chinese reads clear and flowing. Your line: the translator. Today, the strange story told about how his life ended.

A translator's whole life's work rests on one question: did I get it right? Nobody can fully answer that for themselves. Readers decide, slowly, over generations. Kumarajiva, the story goes, asked for a different kind of answer. Near the end of his life, he made a promise in front of his students, and the proof would come only after he was gone, in the fire. Today, a legend: the tongue that did not burn.
screen: `DID I GET IT RIGHT?` → `A PROMISE BEFORE HIS STUDENTS.` → `THE PROOF IN THE FIRE.`

segments.voice: First, the promise. His biography tells it this way. Knowing he was dying, Kumarajiva spoke to the monks around him. He said, in effect: if what I have translated does not betray the meaning of the teaching, then when my body is burned, my tongue will not burn. Second, the fire. After his death, the story says, his body was cremated in the Buddhist way. When the fire died down, his tongue remained, unburned. Third, what the story is saying. It makes its claim in the language of wonder. The tongue is the organ of speech, the thing that spoke every sentence of those translations. For it to survive the fire says, in a picture, that the words were sound. His students, and the readers after them, could point to it. Fourth, how people hold it. Some Buddhists receive the story as a sign. Historians read it as a legend that grew around a translator people already trusted. Tradition says the tongue was enshrined in a pagoda, and a pagoda in the frontier town where he was once held is still linked to it. Either way, the story sits at the very end of his life, after years of readers had already found his Chinese clear and faithful. Readers go on testing a translation slowly, in their own mouths. The story gives his work one vivid image.

905.title: Faxian walks to India
905.hook: the monk Faxian set out on foot for India to find the rules of discipline (Legge, 1886)
905.howItsDone: Buddhist monks and lay pilgrims still travel to the places of the Buddha's life in India and Nepal, and monastic communities study the Vinaya, the rules of discipline Faxian went to find.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the legend of Kumarajiva's tongue, unburned in the fire. Your line: the tongue remained. Today the traffic runs the other way: a Chinese monk heads west.

A monk in Chang'an has a problem with the rulebook. The monks' rules of discipline, the Vinaya, have reached China only in pieces. The books he can find are broken and incomplete, and he wants the whole rulebook. He could wait for someone to bring the rest. Instead, he decides to go and get it himself, on foot, across a desert and over the mountains, all the way to India. And he writes it all down.
screen: `THE RULEBOOK IN PIECES.` → `GO AND GET IT.` → `ON FOOT, TO INDIA.`

segments.voice: First, the reason. Faxian's own record, which James Legge put into English, opens with it. Living in Chang'an, he grieved that the books of discipline in China were broken and incomplete, so he and a few companions agreed to travel to India to seek the rules. Not treasure, not fame. The rulebook. Second, the desert. His record describes a sea of sand with no birds overhead and no animals below, where you look all around and can't tell which way to go. The only markers of the road, he writes, are the dry bones of travelers who died there. Third, the mountains. Beyond the desert came high passes, snow in winter and summer, cliffs where the path was cut into the rock and the river ran far below. Along the way companions turned back, fell ill, or stayed behind in monasteries. Faxian kept walking. Fourth, India. He reached the places of the Buddha's life, the holy sites he had only read about, and settled down to study and copy texts of the discipline, so he could carry them home. What makes his record matter is that it isn't a legend told by others. It's a traveler's own account, plain and specific, of what he saw: monasteries, customs, rulers, the state of the holy places. Historians still read it for that reason. And at its center is one stubborn decision: he wanted the rules whole.

906.title: The fan from home
906.hook: in Sri Lanka Faxian sees a merchant offer a Chinese fan and weeps with homesickness
906.howItsDone: Buddhist pilgrims and monks who travel far to study often keep in touch with home through letters, offerings and small gifts, and travelers' records like Faxian's are read as part of the tradition's history.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Faxian set out on foot across the desert and the mountains to find the rules of discipline. Your line: he walked to India. Today, far from home, the walker stops.

A white silk fan. That's all it is. A merchant steps up to a great image of the Buddha in a monastery in Sri Lanka and lays it down as an offering. Nobody around him would look twice. But a Chinese monk standing beside the image looks, and keeps looking. The fan is from China, something from home after years away. And the man who crossed a desert marked by bones, who climbed passes of snow, starts to cry.
screen: `A WHITE SILK FAN.` → `AN OFFERING IN SRI LANKA.` → `THE WALKER WEEPS.`

segments.voice: First, how he got there. After his years of study in India, Faxian took ship to Sri Lanka, the island on the southern road, and stayed there to find more texts. In one monastery stood a large image of the Buddha in green jade. Second, what he wrote. In Legge's translation, Faxian describes his state of mind before the fan. Many years had passed since he left China. The people around him were all from other lands. His eyes had not rested on a familiar hill or river, plant or tree. His companions were gone, some dead, some scattered. He was alone, and sadness stayed with him. Third, the moment. By the image he saw the merchant offer a white silk fan from China, and tears filled his eyes and fell. That's the whole scene. He doesn't explain it away; he just sets it down in his record. Fourth, why it matters that he wrote it. Faxian was a monk on a serious errand, a man trained in letting go. And here he is, undone by a fan, and he leaves the moment in. Buddhist teaching speaks plainly about attachment and the pain of separation from what we love. Faxian's page doesn't argue with that teaching. It shows what it can look like from the inside, in a temple, far from home, holding nothing but his own sorrow. And then, the record says, he went on with his work.

907.title: Xuanzang crosses the desert
907.hook: a monk goes west alone, against an imperial ban, and loses his water in the sand
907.howItsDone: Chinese Buddhists remember Xuanzang as a model pilgrim and translator, and his journey to India is retold in stories and plays.

segments.voice: Yesterday: attachment, and Faxian's tears over a fan from home. Your line: a fan from home. Today another monk takes the road west, and this one goes without permission.

The sand drinks it in seconds: a full leather water bag, tipped from a tired hand. In his biography, that's the moment the monk Xuanzang finds himself beyond China's western border with no water and a long way still to go. He isn't supposed to be there. The government had forbidden travel out of the country, and he left anyway, slipping past the watchtowers at night. He was going to India for Buddhist texts, whole and in their own language, so he could stop guessing at what the Chinese versions meant.
screen: `A WATER BAG SPILLS INTO THE SAND.` → `NO PERMISSION TO LEAVE.` → `XUANZANG CROSSES THE DESERT.`

segments.voice: First, why he went. Xuanzang was a young monk who had studied with teachers across China, and the teachers didn't agree. Neither did the translations he had. He wanted the source. Second, how he left. He asked for permission to travel and was refused. He went anyway. His biography, written by his disciple Huili, says a guide set out with him, then lost his nerve and turned back. An old man traded him a thin red horse that, the old man said, had made the crossing many times. So Xuanzang went on alone, with a horse that knew the way better than he did. Third, the water. After the bag spilled, he did the sensible thing: he turned back east, toward the last watchtower. Then he stopped. The biography says he remembered a vow he had made: not to take one step back toward the east until he reached India. He turned the horse west again. For days he went without water, until he lay down in the sand. Tradition says he called on Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion, and recited the Heart Sutra. In the night a cool wind woke him, and the old horse pulled toward a patch of grass and a pool. Fourth, what the story is about. It isn't about having no fear. He was afraid enough to turn around. The brave part was small. Courage can be that size: one turn of the reins, back toward where you meant to go.

908.title: Xuanzang at Nalanda
908.hook: after deserts and mountains, the traveler sits down and becomes a student again
908.howItsDone: In monastic schools of several Buddhist traditions, students still study a few core texts slowly with a teacher, memorizing, discussing and debating them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Xuanzang crossed the desert, lost his water, and turned his horse west again. Your line: alone across the sand.

What does a person do after crossing deserts and mountain passes to reach the place he set out for? Throw a party? Write home? Xuanzang became a student again. He reached Nalanda, the great monastery of learning in north India that this path visited earlier this year, and instead of collecting texts and hurrying back, he stayed. He learned the language. He sat in lectures. He read the same difficult books over and over. Today, Nalanda through one pair of eyes: a guest from China who made it his school.
screen: `THE TRAVELER ARRIVES.` → `HE STAYS.` → `NALANDA THROUGH ONE PAIR OF EYES.`

segments.voice: First, the teacher who was waiting. The head of Nalanda in Xuanzang's day was an old monk named Shilabhadra, deeply honored there, his biography says. And it tells a striking story: years before, Shilabhadra had been ill and in pain, and in a dream he was told to bear it, because a monk from China would come to learn from him. When Xuanzang arrived, the story of that dream was told to him. Second, what he came to learn. Shilabhadra taught the Yogacara, a school whose great subject is the mind: how what we experience is shaped by the mind that experiences it. Xuanzang had come for one long text of that school in particular, and he heard it taught from beginning to end. Third, life inside the walls. The biography describes monks discussing and debating from morning until night, rooms given to guests, and food supplied so the students could study. Xuanzang learned Sanskrit well enough to read, argue and later translate. Fourth, why it matters. He could have filled his bags and left. He stayed for years, because some things don't open on a first reading. The Dhammapada, the Buddha's sayings, begins with a line that points the same way: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought." A line like that is easy to say and slow to understand. Depth can look like this: coming back to the same thing until it gives up what it has.

909.title: Home with the texts
909.hook: Xuanzang comes home with the texts and spends his life translating; centuries later he becomes the monk in Journey to the West
909.howItsDone: Xuanzang's translations are still read in Chinese Buddhist communities, and Journey to the West is retold in operas, films and comics.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Xuanzang at Nalanda, the traveler who stopped to study with an old teacher. Your line: years at Nalanda.

A monkey who can somersault across the sky. A pig with a rake and a big appetite. A quiet giant from a river. And in the middle of them, riding a white horse, a gentle monk heading west for scriptures. If you've seen a cartoon, a TV series or a video game about the Monkey King, you've met Xuanzang, or a version of him. The real monk walked home with his texts. The legend gave him a monkey. Today, both.
screen: `A MONKEY, A PIG, A RIVER GIANT.` → `A MONK ON A WHITE HORSE.` → `HOME WITH THE TEXTS.`

segments.voice: First, the homecoming. Xuanzang had left China against a ban. He came back with horses loaded with Buddhist texts in Sanskrit, along with images and relics, and his biography describes crowds lining the way into the capital. The emperor, instead of punishing him, received him and asked him to write down everything he had seen in the western lands. That book still exists; its English translator called it Buddhist Records of the Western World. Second, the rest of his life. Xuanzang spent his remaining years translating with teams of monks, turning what he had carried home into Chinese. A version of the short Heart Sutra still chanted in Chinese is traditionally credited to him. The desert crossing was one journey. The translating took the rest of his life. Third, the legend. Long after his death, storytellers kept his journey going, and it grew into a long novel, Journey to the West. In it the monk is called Tripitaka, and he's protected on the road by a band of strange disciples: Monkey, born from a stone, clever and impossible to control; Pigsy; Sandy; and a dragon who has become his horse. Fourth, what the monkey might mean. Some readers see Monkey as the restless mind, brilliant, quick, always leaping off somewhere, and the monk as the steady purpose that keeps the whole party walking west. Whatever the novel intends, the pair is easy to spot in any busy day: the leaping thought, and the slow walk forward.

910.title: The Chinese schools
910.hook: Tiantai, Huayan, Chan, Pure Land: a first look at four Chinese schools, with no ranking
910.howItsDone: In Chinese Buddhist temples today, practices from these schools often sit side by side: sutra study, sitting meditation, and chanting the name of Amitabha Buddha.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Xuanzang came home with the texts, and a novel later named him Tripitaka and gave him a monkey for company. Your line: the monkey and the monk.

Four names, said slowly. Tiantai. Huayan. Chan. Pure Land. Translators like Kumarajiva had filled Chinese libraries with sutras, and the sutras didn't all say the same thing. Some taught emptiness, some praised a Buddha in a distant land, some described whole universes inside a speck of dust. Chinese teachers asked a fair question: how does all of this fit together? Different teachers answered in different ways, and schools grew up around their answers. Today, a first look at four of them, none ranked above another.
screen: `FOUR NAMES.` → `SO MANY SUTRAS.` → `HOW DOES IT FIT TOGETHER?`

segments.voice: First, Tiantai. It's named after a mountain, Mount Tiantai, where the teacher Zhiyi lived and taught. Tiantai puts the Lotus Sutra at the center, and it tries to hold all the Buddha's teachings in one big order, as one teaching given in different ways to different listeners, the way a good teacher explains the same idea to a child and to a scholar. Second, Huayan, which means flower garland, after the Flower Garland Sutra. Its great picture is connection: every thing in the universe reflects every other thing, the way jewels in a net catch each other's light. Third, Chan. Tradition hears in the name the Sanskrit word dhyana, meditation. Chan trusts sitting and direct seeing over long study, and its teachers tell sharp, surprising stories. Later it would travel to Korea as Seon and to Japan as Zen. Fourth, Pure Land. Its center is Amitabha, the Buddha of boundless light, who in the sutras vows to welcome into his Pure Land anyone who calls on him with faith. Its practice is simple and can be done anywhere: reciting his name. One more thing. In China these schools were often not walled off from one another. One monastery might hold Chan sitting in the morning and Pure Land chanting in the evening, under the same roof. They're less like rival teams than like rooms in one house.
screen: `TIANTAI: A MOUNTAIN AND THE LOTUS.` · `HUAYAN: THE FLOWER GARLAND.` · `CHAN: SITTING AND DIRECT SEEING.` · `PURE LAND: CALLING AMITABHA'S NAME.` · then, large: `FOUR CHINESE SCHOOLS.`

segments.voice: Breathe out on each name in turn: Tiantai, with the mountain and the Lotus; Huayan, with the net of jewels; Chan, with a few breaths of simply sitting; Pure Land, with the Buddha of boundless light. Then rest in the breath with no names at all.
